subject_home_community.label: Swinging Big Band Era
subject_home_community.summary: This community centers on the apex of the big band era and the subsequent rise of bebop, dominated by major bandleaders and virtuoso soloists who defined mainstream jazz. Members are bound by extensive professional collaborations in touring orchestras and the vibrant New York and Chicago club scenes during the mid-20th century.
subject_home_community.note: Randy Weston (wd:Q1371187) sits in this community -- the same one as John Coltrane, Miles Davis and Melba Liston, the other 1926 centennials.

method.communities: All rows of `communities` (seeded Louvain, labels/era/place/scene/summary are LLM-generated with a confidence score). key_figures parsed from its JSON array. Sorted by rank asc. is_subject_home flags community 2.
method.home_members: Top 60 nodes with community = 2 ordered by nodes.mentions desc (ties by docs desc, then label), enriched with wd_people description/dates/portrait and node_collections.

communities.label: Post-War Hard Bop & Bebop
communities.scene: Hard bop, bebop, and post-bop jazz network
communities.summary: This community centers on the hard bop and post-bop movements that dominated jazz from the 1950s through the 1970s, characterized by a dense network of New York-based musicians, educators, and archivists. The group is bound by shared performance histories in the bebop and hard bop scenes, featuring key figures like Mingus, Golson, and McLean who defined the genre's aesthetic and institutional legacy.

communities.label: Swinging Big Band Era
communities.scene: Mainstream swing and bebop transition
communities.summary: This community centers on the apex of the big band era and the subsequent rise of bebop, dominated by major bandleaders and virtuoso soloists who defined mainstream jazz. Members are bound by extensive professional collaborations in touring orchestras and the vibrant New York and Chicago club scenes during the mid-20th century.

communities.label: Chicago-style Dixieland Revival
communities.scene: Traditional jazz revival and swing era big bands
communities.summary: This community centers on the Chicago-style Dixieland revival and the swing era, characterized by musicians who preserved early New Orleans traditions while dominating the 1930s-40s big band and small-group scenes. Key figures like Eddie Condon and Jimmy McPartland formed a tight social circle in Chicago and New York, bridging the gap between early jazz pioneers and the post-war traditional jazz revival.

communities.label: Bebop and Cool Jazz Elite
communities.scene: Post-war bebop, cool jazz, and high-profile entertainment circles
communities.summary: This community centers on the innovators of bebop and cool jazz who dominated the New York scene from the late 1940s through the 1960s. It binds together pioneering instrumentalists, arrangers, and bandleaders with high-profile entertainers and cultural figures who shared the same elite performance venues and recording sessions.

communities.label: Early Blues & Jazz Pioneers
communities.scene: Delta blues, boogie-woogie, and early jazz
communities.summary: This community represents the foundational figures of American blues and early jazz, spanning from the late 19th-century roots in New Orleans to the Chicago blues boom of the 1930s and 40s. It binds together pioneers of boogie-woogie, country blues, and jazz who established the stylistic templates for 20th-century popular music.

communities.label: New Orleans Jazz & Negro League Stars
communities.scene: Territory bands, brass-band revival, and Negro league sports
communities.summary: This community centers on the New Orleans jazz ecosystem of the 1920s and 30s, characterized by territory bands and brass-band traditions. It is uniquely bound by the social overlap between jazz musicians and Negro league baseball stars, who frequently toured together and shared performance circuits in cities like New Orleans, Harlem, and San Antonio.

communities.label: Kansas City Swing & Territory Bands
communities.scene: Territory band circuit and big band swing era
communities.summary: This community centers on the Kansas City jazz scene and the broader 'territory band' circuit of the 1930s and 40s, characterized by long-running ensemble work and a distinct, riff-based swing style. Key figures like Buster Smith and Jay McShann represent the foundational Kansas City sound, while members like Jo Jones and Buck Clayton highlight the migration of this style into major big bands like Count Basie's. The network reflects the interconnected social and professional web of musicians who toured the Midwest and South before settling in major urban hubs.

communities.label: New Orleans Brass Band Tradition
communities.scene: Traditional jazz and brass band musicians
communities.summary: This community consists of core figures in the New Orleans traditional jazz and brass band scene, active primarily from the early 20th century through the mid-century revival. Members are linked by direct professional associations, familial ties, and shared participation in iconic local ensembles like the Olympia Brass Band and Eureka Brass Band.

communities.label: NYC Late Show & Studio Elite
communities.scene: Late Night television bands and high-profile studio session musicians
communities.summary: This community centers on the core musicians of the CBS Orchestra (Late Show with David Letterman) and the broader New York studio session elite who facilitated cross-genre collaborations. The network is anchored by the Jazz Foundation of America, linking these high-profile performers with archival preservation efforts and historical figures like Alcide Pavageau.

communities.label: New Orleans Brass & Blues Network
communities.scene: Early jazz, brass bands, and blues
communities.summary: This community centers on the foundational figures of New Orleans jazz and blues, linking brass band leaders, early recording artists, and blues pioneers. It captures the social and musical network of the early 20th century, highlighting the transition from ragtime and brass bands to the recorded jazz and blues era.

communities.label: Vaudeville and Tin Pan Alley
communities.scene: Broadway musicals, vaudeville, and popular songwriting
communities.summary: This community centers on the commercial popular music and theater industry of the early 20th century, specifically Broadway and vaudeville. It binds together songwriters, composers, and performers who shaped the Great American Songbook and stage musicals, distinct from the pure jazz or classical scenes.

communities.label: New Orleans R&B and Jazz Hub
communities.scene: Studio musicians, brass bands, and R&B pioneers
communities.summary: This community centers on the New Orleans music ecosystem, specifically the intersection of traditional jazz, brass bands, and the R&B/rock and roll boom of the mid-20th century. Members are bound by professional collaborations in local recording studios (notably Cosimo Matassa's) and shared performance circuits, linking legendary session players, bandleaders, and educators.

communities.label: New Orleans Jazz Oral History
communities.scene: Traditional jazz and brass band network
communities.summary: This community centers on the traditional jazz and brass band scene of New Orleans, primarily documented through 1948-1997 field interviews. It binds musicians, journalists, and educators who were active or interviewed regarding the city's early 20th-century musical heritage.

communities.label: New Orleans Jazz Pioneers
communities.scene: Early jazz, brass bands, and Creole musical networks
communities.summary: This community represents the foundational generation of New Orleans jazz, centered on the city's brass band traditions and the mentorship networks that defined early 20th-century American music. It binds together the Creole of color classical musicians, the ragtime and blues pioneers, and the first generation of jazz stars who emerged from the social and musical milieu of New Orleans.

communities.label: Dixieland Revival & Western Swing
communities.scene: Traditional jazz revivalists and Western Swing pioneers
communities.summary: This community bridges the traditional New Orleans jazz revival (led by figures like Watkins and Edegran) with the Western Swing and country music scene (Wills, Acuff). It is defined by the cross-pollination of early 20th-century vernacular music styles, where Dixieland musicians and country/western bandleaders are linked through shared oral histories and performance networks.

communities.label: Transcendentalist & Jazz Intellectuals
communities.scene: 19th-century Transcendentalism and 20th-century Jazz history
communities.summary: This community is an artifact of data contamination, linking 19th-century New England Transcendentalists with 20th-century jazz figures through erroneous network edges. The core consists of the Alcott circle and Henry David Thoreau, incorrectly connected to jazz historians and musicians like James Lincoln Collier and Dave Barbour. The binding factor is not musical collaboration but likely shared mentions in literary or biographical texts within the oral history archives.

communities.label: Swing Era New Orleans Jazz
communities.scene: New Orleans brass band and swing tradition
communities.summary: This community centers on the New Orleans jazz tradition, specifically the brass band and swing era styles that defined the city's musical output from the 1930s through the 1950s. Members are primarily musicians who performed in local ensembles or toured with major acts, maintaining strong ties to the New Orleans musical lineage.

communities.label: LA Session & Jazz Fusion
communities.scene: Wrecking Crew session musicians and jazz fusion
communities.summary: This community centers on the elite Los Angeles session musician circuit, prominently featuring members of the Wrecking Crew and their extended network. It bridges the gap between 1960s pop/rock production and the smoother jazz and fusion styles that emerged in subsequent decades.

communities.label: 1940s New Orleans Jazz Circle
communities.scene: Traditional jazz and brass band network
communities.summary: This community represents the core network of traditional New Orleans jazz musicians active during the mid-20th century, heavily documented in the Tulane/Hogan oral history archives. The members are bound by direct professional associations and mutual recognition within the local brass band and jazz scene, reflecting the enduring social fabric of New Orleans music culture.

communities.label: Broadway & Vaudeville Jazz Elite
communities.scene: Blackface and integrated musical theater, tap dance, and blues vaudeville
communities.summary: This community centers on the intersection of African American vernacular performance (tap, blues, vaudeville) and white-dominated Broadway musical theater production during the early 20th century. It binds together pioneering Black entertainers like Bill Robinson and Alberta Hunter with major white producers and composers such as Jerome Kern and Oscar Hammerstein, reflecting the collaborative yet segregated dynamics of the era's entertainment industry.

communities.label: New Orleans Jazz & Post-War Connections
communities.scene: Traditional New Orleans jazz musicians and their post-war diaspora networks
communities.summary: This community centers on traditional New Orleans jazz musicians active from the 1920s through the 1960s, anchored by local figures like Julius Handy and Walter Benoit. It extends to key diaspora connections, notably trumpeter Joe Gordon, who linked the New Orleans scene to the broader American jazz circuit in Boston and New York. The network reflects the oral history of a specific generation of brass-band and traditional jazz players.

communities.label: Parisian Jazz & Negritude Circle
communities.scene: African American expatriate jazz musicians and Francophone literary/intellectual elites
communities.summary: This community centers on the vibrant Parisian jazz scene of the interwar and post-war periods, dominated by African American expatriate musicians like Arthur Briggs and Jacques Butler who found artistic freedom in France. It is uniquely bound by deep social and intellectual ties to the Négritude movement and French existentialist circles, evidenced by the presence of figures like Aimé Césaire, Léopold Sédar Senghor, and Jean-Paul Sartre alongside the musicians.

communities.label: Swing Era Studio & Radio Musicians
communities.scene: Big band, radio orchestras, and studio session players
communities.summary: This community consists of prominent bandleaders, arrangers, and studio musicians who defined the Swing and Easy Listening eras, primarily centered in New York. The network is bound by professional collaborations in radio broadcasts, big band recordings, and the lucrative 52nd Street studio scene. It bridges the gap between traditional jazz figures and the commercial pop-orchestral sounds that dominated mid-century American media.

communities.label: Classic Blues & Ragtime Era
communities.scene: Vaudeville blues singers and ragtime pianists
communities.summary: This community centers on the Classic Blues era and ragtime piano tradition, linking the 'Empress of the Blues' and vaudeville performers with New Orleans clarinetists and early ragtime composers. They are bound by the pre-bebop jazz and blues circuit of the early 20th century, where blues vocalists and pianists often crossed paths in touring circuits and recording sessions.

communities.label: Pre-Jazz New Orleans Elite
communities.scene: Late 19th-century civic and social circles
communities.summary: This community represents the pre-jazz civic and social elite of New Orleans in the late 19th century, centered around figures like Police Chief David Hennessy. The connections reflect social networks of authority and respectability rather than a musical performance scene, as the median birth year of 1858 places these individuals in their prime during the 1880s and 1890s, prior to the emergence of jazz.

communities.label: 1948-1997 New Orleans Jazz
communities.scene: Traditional jazz and brass band revival
communities.summary: This community comprises musicians and figures active in New Orleans' traditional jazz and brass band scenes between 1948 and 1997. They are bound by oral history interviews conducted by Tulane University, focusing on personal connections and professional collaborations within the local music ecosystem.

communities.label: Post-Bop Bassists & Producers
communities.scene: Hard bop and post-bop jazz network
communities.summary: This community centers on the post-bop jazz scene, anchored by prominent double-bassists like Walter Booker and Marshall Hawkins who were active in major US hubs like New York and Washington D.C. The inclusion of Dusty Springfield and producer Richard Seidel suggests a crossover into broader soul-jazz or pop-jazz production circles, linking the rigid jazz interview network to wider musical collaborations.

communities.label: New Orleans Brass Band Revivalists
communities.scene: Traditional jazz revival and brass band culture
communities.summary: This community comprises musicians and figures central to the New Orleans traditional jazz revival, heavily documented in the Tulane/Hogan oral history archives. They are bound by a shared commitment to preserving early jazz styles, particularly through brass bands and street performances, spanning from the mid-20th century into the late 1990s.

communities.label: 1948-1997 New Orleans Jazz Elders
communities.scene: Oral history preservation of traditional jazz
communities.summary: This community consists of eight individuals identified solely through oral history interviews conducted at Tulane University between 1948 and 1997. The group represents a tight-knit circle of New Orleans jazz musicians and figures whose connections are defined by mutual recognition and shared performance history rather than widespread public fame.

communities.label: New York Avant-Garde & Blues

communities.summary: This community centers on the New York jazz scene of the mid-20th century, specifically bridging the gap between traditional blues figures and the emerging avant-garde movement. It is defined by the interactions between pioneering bebop/cool jazz pianists, free jazz saxophonists, and the literary/intellectual circles (including writers and producers) that supported and documented this cultural shift.

communities.label: 1930s British Dance Band Era

communities.summary: This community is defined by the British dance band era of the 1930s, centered on bandleaders and vocalists who dominated the UK entertainment scene. While Nelson Eddy was an American crossover star, his inclusion alongside British bandleaders Jack Payne and Nat Gonella suggests a network focused on the popular, accessible jazz and pop music that bridged classical and popular tastes during this period.

communities.label: New Orleans Jazz & Blues Network

The group is bound by direct associations among key figures of the brass-band, jug band, and Delta blues traditions who were active in the region during the 1920s and 1930s.

communities.place: New York City and New Orleans

communities.summary: This community centers on the fusion of Afro-Cuban rhythms with American jazz, pioneered by figures like Mario Bauza and Chico O’Farrill in New York. It connects Cuban and Puerto Rican musicians with New Orleans jazz traditions, highlighting the cross-pollination between Latin jazz and traditional jazz scenes.

communities.scene: Traditional jazz and brass-band revivalists
communities.summary: This community centers on the New Orleans traditional jazz and Dixieland revival scene, featuring musicians who preserved or revived early brass-band styles. communities.summary: This community consists of a single identified node, Aldo Moro, an Italian statesman and former Prime Minister. The data indicates a severe mismatch between the jazz oral history context and the subject, as Moro was a politician with no known connection to the jazz musicians described in the archives.

communities.summary: This community connects pioneering African American performers spanning vaudeville, classical concert, blues, and gospel traditions. It is bound by the shared experience of Black artists navigating the American entertainment industry from the early 20th century through the civil rights era, with strong ties to New Orleans and Chicago.

communities.summary: This community centers on the Berklee College of Music faculty and alumni network, specifically linking tenor saxophonist Andy McGhee with his student Bill Pierce. It bridges the gap between the academic jazz education scene in Boston and the funk/soul saxophone tradition established by James Brown sidemen like Pee Wee Ellis and Maceo Parker.

Members are bound by professional collaborations in local recording studios (notably Cosimo Matassa's) and shared performance circuits, linking legendary session players, bandleaders, and educators.

items.label: New Orleans Jazz Oral History
items.scene: Traditional jazz and brass band network
items.summary: This community centers on the traditional jazz and brass band scene of New Orleans, primarily documented through 1948-1997 field interviews. It binds musicians, journalists, and educators who were active or interviewed regarding the city's early 20th-century musical heritage.

items.label: New Orleans Jazz Pioneers
items.scene: Early jazz, brass bands, and Creole musical networks
items.summary: This community represents the foundational generation of New Orleans jazz, centered on the city's brass band traditions and the mentorship networks that defined early 20th-century American music. It binds together the Creole of color classical musicians, the ragtime and blues pioneers, and the first generation of jazz stars who emerged from the social and musical milieu of New Orleans.

items.label: Dixieland Revival & Western Swing
items.scene: Traditional jazz revivalists and Western Swing pioneers
items.summary: This community bridges the traditional New Orleans jazz revival (led by figures like Watkins and Edegran) with the Western Swing and country music scene (Wills, Acuff). It is defined by the cross-pollination of early 20th-century vernacular music styles, where Dixieland musicians and country/western bandleaders are linked through shared oral histories and performance networks.

items.label: Transcendentalist & Jazz Intellectuals
items.scene: 19th-century Transcendentalism and 20th-century Jazz history
items.summary: This community is an artifact of data contamination, linking 19th-century New England Transcendentalists with 20th-century jazz figures through erroneous network edges. The core consists of the Alcott circle and Henry David Thoreau, incorrectly connected to jazz historians and musicians like James Lincoln Collier and Dave Barbour. The binding factor is not musical collaboration but likely shared mentions in literary or biographical texts within the oral history archives.

items.label: Swing Era New Orleans Jazz
items.scene: New Orleans brass band and swing tradition
items.summary: This community centers on the New Orleans jazz tradition, specifically the brass band and swing era styles that defined the city's musical output from the 1930s through the 1950s. Members are primarily musicians who performed in local ensembles or toured with major acts, maintaining strong ties to the New Orleans musical lineage.

items.label: LA Session & Jazz Fusion
items.scene: Wrecking Crew session musicians and jazz fusion
items.summary: This community centers on the elite Los Angeles session musician circuit, prominently featuring members of the Wrecking Crew and their extended network. It bridges the gap between 1960s pop/rock production and the smoother jazz and fusion styles that emerged in subsequent decades.

items.label: 1940s New Orleans Jazz Circle
items.scene: Traditional jazz and brass band network
items.summary: This community represents the core network of traditional New Orleans jazz musicians active during the mid-20th century, heavily documented in the Tulane/Hogan oral history archives. The members are bound by direct professional associations and mutual recognition within the local brass band and jazz scene, reflecting the enduring social fabric of New Orleans music culture.

items.label: Broadway & Vaudeville Jazz Elite
items.scene: Blackface and integrated musical theater, tap dance, and blues vaudeville
items.summary: This community centers on the intersection of African American vernacular performance (tap, blues, vaudeville) and white-dominated Broadway musical theater production during the early 20th century. It binds together pioneering Black entertainers like Bill Robinson and Alberta Hunter with major white producers and composers such as Jerome Kern and Oscar Hammerstein, reflecting the collaborative yet segregated dynamics of the era's entertainment industry.

items.label: New Orleans Jazz & Post-War Connections
items.scene: Traditional New Orleans jazz musicians and their post-war diaspora networks
items.summary: This community centers on traditional New Orleans jazz musicians active from the 1920s through the 1960s, anchored by local figures like Julius Handy and Walter Benoit. It extends to key diaspora connections, notably trumpeter Joe Gordon, who linked the New Orleans scene to the broader American jazz circuit in Boston and New York. The network reflects the oral history of a specific generation of brass-band and traditional jazz players.

items.label: Parisian Jazz & Negritude Circle
items.scene: African American expatriate jazz musicians and Francophone literary/intellectual elites
items.summary: This community centers on the vibrant Parisian jazz scene of the interwar and post-war periods, dominated by African American expatriate musicians like Arthur Briggs and Jacques Butler who found artistic freedom in France. It is uniquely bound by deep social and intellectual ties to the Négritude movement and French existentialist circles, evidenced by the presence of figures like Aimé Césaire, Léopold Sédar Senghor, and Jean-Paul Sartre alongside the musicians.

items.label: Swing Era Studio & Radio Musicians
items.scene: Big band, radio orchestras, and studio session players
items.summary: This community consists of prominent bandleaders, arrangers, and studio musicians who defined the Swing and Easy Listening eras, primarily centered in New York. The network is bound by professional collaborations in radio broadcasts, big band recordings, and the lucrative 52nd Street studio scene. It bridges the gap between traditional jazz figures and the commercial pop-orchestral sounds that dominated mid-century American media.

items.label: Classic Blues & Ragtime Era
items.scene: Vaudeville blues singers and ragtime pianists
items.summary: This community centers on the Classic Blues era and ragtime piano tradition, linking the 'Empress of the Blues' and vaudeville performers with New Orleans clarinetists and early ragtime composers. They are bound by the pre-bebop jazz and blues circuit of the early 20th century, where blues vocalists and pianists often crossed paths in touring circuits and recording sessions.

items.label: Pre-Jazz New Orleans Elite
items.scene: Late 19th-century civic and social circles
items.summary: This community represents the pre-jazz civic and social elite of New Orleans in the late 19th century, centered around figures like Police Chief David Hennessy. The connections reflect social networks of authority and respectability rather than a musical performance scene, as the median birth year of 1858 places these individuals in their prime during the 1880s and 1890s, prior to the emergence of jazz.

items.label: 1948-1997 New Orleans Jazz
items.scene: Traditional jazz and brass band revival
items.summary: This community comprises musicians and figures active in New Orleans' traditional jazz and brass band scenes between 1948 and 1997. They are bound by oral history interviews conducted by Tulane University, focusing on personal connections and professional collaborations within the local music ecosystem.

items.label: Post-Bop Bassists & Producers
items.scene: Hard bop and post-bop jazz network
items.summary: This community centers on the post-bop jazz scene, anchored by prominent double-bassists like Walter Booker and Marshall Hawkins who were active in major US hubs like New York and Washington D.C. The inclusion of Dusty Springfield and producer Richard Seidel suggests a crossover into broader soul-jazz or pop-jazz production circles, linking the rigid jazz interview network to wider musical collaborations.

items.label: New Orleans Brass Band Revivalists
items.scene: Traditional jazz revival and brass band culture
items.summary: This community comprises musicians and figures central to the New Orleans traditional jazz revival, heavily documented in the Tulane/Hogan oral history archives. They are bound by a shared commitment to preserving early jazz styles, particularly through brass bands and street performances, spanning from the mid-20th century into the late 1990s.

items.label: 1948-1997 New Orleans Jazz Elders
items.scene: Oral history preservation of traditional jazz
items.summary: This community consists of eight individuals identified solely through oral history interviews conducted at Tulane University between 1948 and 1997. The group represents a tight-knit circle of New Orleans jazz musicians and figures whose connections are defined by mutual recognition and shared performance history rather than widespread public fame.

items.label: New York Avant-Garde & Blues
items.scene: Avant-garde jazz, blues revival, and literary circles
items.summary: This community centers on the New York jazz scene of the mid-20th century, specifically bridging the gap between traditional blues figures and the emerging avant-garde movement. It is defined by the interactions between pioneering bebop/cool jazz pianists, free jazz saxophonists, and the literary/intellectual circles (including writers and producers) that supported and documented this cultural shift.

items.label: 1930s British Dance Band Era
items.scene: British dance band and vocal crossover stars
items.summary: This community is defined by the British dance band era of the 1930s, centered on bandleaders and vocalists who dominated the UK entertainment scene. While Nelson Eddy was an American crossover star, his inclusion alongside British bandleaders Jack Payne and Nat Gonella suggests a network focused on the popular, accessible jazz and pop music that bridged classical and popular tastes during this period.

items.label: New Orleans Jazz & Blues Network
items.scene: Early jazz, blues, and jug band scene
items.summary: This community centers on the early 20th-century New Orleans jazz and blues scene, characterized by the dense social and professional networks of pioneering musicians. The group is bound by direct associations among key figures of the brass-band, jug band, and Delta blues traditions who were active in the region during the 1920s and 1930s.

items.label: Afro-Cuban Jazz & Latin Jazz
items.place: New York City and New Orleans
items.scene: Afro-Cuban jazz, Cubop, and Latin jazz fusion
items.summary: This community centers on the fusion of Afro-Cuban rhythms with American jazz, pioneered by figures like Mario Bauza and Chico O’Farrill in New York. It connects Cuban and Puerto Rican musicians with New Orleans jazz traditions, highlighting the cross-pollination between Latin jazz and traditional jazz scenes.

items.label: New Orleans Dixieland Revival
items.scene: Traditional jazz and brass-band revivalists
items.summary: This community centers on the New Orleans traditional jazz and Dixieland revival scene, featuring musicians who preserved or revived early brass-band styles. The network is anchored by key figures from the 1920s-1940s who maintained strong ties to the New Orleans musical heritage, often performing in local clubs or leading revival bands.

items.label: Cool Jazz and Avant-Garde
items.scene: West Coast cool jazz, classical crossover, and intellectual jazz circles
items.summary: This community centers on the 'cool jazz' movement and its intellectual/classical intersections, dominated by the Dave Brubeck Quartet and their circle. It binds mid-century jazz musicians with classical composers, record executives, and cultural figures who valued complex time signatures and cross-genre experimentation.

items.label: 1948-1997 New Orleans Jazz
items.scene: Tulane Oral History field interviews
items.summary: This community consists of individuals connected through oral history interviews conducted by Tulane University between 1948 and 1997. The network reflects recollections of knowing or playing with other musicians, centered entirely on the New Orleans jazz scene during this period.

items.label: Italian Politician
items.scene: Italian Christian Democracy politics
items.summary: This community consists of a single identified node, Aldo Moro, an Italian statesman and former Prime Minister. The data indicates a severe mismatch between the jazz oral history context and the subject, as Moro was a politician with no known connection to the jazz musicians described in the archives.

items.label: Motown and Soul Executives
items.scene: Motown Records and R&B industry elite
items.summary: This community centers on the architects and stars of the Motown sound and the broader R&B/soul industry of the 1960s and 70s. The connections are driven by record executives, producers, and hit-making artists who defined the commercial soul music era.

items.label: New Orleans Brass Band Revivalists
items.scene: Traditional jazz revival and brass band culture
items.summary: This community centers on the New Orleans traditional jazz revival, featuring veteran musicians who maintained the city's brass band and early jazz traditions from the 1940s through the late 20th century. The network is heavily anchored by Tulane/Hogan Archive interviews, highlighting a tight-knit circle of elders who preserved and performed historic styles well into the modern era.

items.label: Gospel, Blues & Vaudeville Icons
items.scene: African American performance arts and gospel/blues networks
items.summary: This community connects pioneering African American performers spanning vaudeville, classical concert, blues, and gospel traditions. It is bound by the shared experience of Black artists navigating the American entertainment industry from the early 20th century through the civil rights era, with strong ties to New Orleans and Chicago.

items.label: Berklee Jazz Educators & Funk Saxophonists
items.scene: Academic jazz pedagogy and funk/soul saxophone lineage
items.summary: This community centers on the Berklee College of Music faculty and alumni network, specifically linking tenor saxophonist Andy McGhee with his student Bill Pierce. It bridges the gap between the academic jazz education scene in Boston and the funk/soul saxophone tradition established by James Brown sidemen like Pee Wee Ellis and Maceo Parker.

items.label: 1908 New Orleans Jazz & Blues Circle
items.scene: Early jazz and classic blues social network
items.summary: This community centers on musicians active in New Orleans during the early 20th century, specifically anchored by the birth year 1908. It connects early jazz trombonist Henderson Chambers with classic blues singer Cleo Gibson, reflecting the intertwined social and performance circles of New Orleans' foundational jazz and blues scenes.

items.label: 1948 New Orleans Jazz Field Interviews
items.scene: Traditional jazz and brass band community
items.summary: This community consists of individuals connected through oral history interviews conducted in New Orleans between 1948 and 1997, primarily focusing on the traditional jazz and brass band scenes of the mid-20th century. The tight clustering and single birth year suggest a specific cohort of musicians and associates active during the post-war revival of New Orleans jazz styles.

items.label: New Orleans Brass Band Pioneers

items.summary: This community consists of foundational New Orleans musicians and educators active during the formative years of jazz. They are bound by their participation in the local brass band and early jazz scene, with connections documented through oral histories spanning several decades.

items.summary: This community consists of musicians and figures active in New Orleans during the mid-20th century, primarily connected through oral history interviews conducted by the Hogan Jazz Archive. items.summary: This community comprises musicians and figures central to the New Orleans traditional jazz revival, particularly those active in the city's brass band and street parade traditions. The network reflects a dense web of personal and professional connections among veterans who preserved and performed early jazz styles from the mid-20th century onwards.

items.label: 90s Rock Producers & Media

items.summary: This community consists of prominent rock producers, session musicians, and media personalities active primarily from the 1980s through the 2000s. items.label: Swing Era Big Band Leaders
items.scene: Harlem Renaissance big band orchestras and swing
items.summary: This community centers on the architects of the Swing Era, specifically the large ensemble orchestras that defined Harlem's nightlife and national popular music between the 1920s and 1940s. Members are predominantly bandleaders, arrangers, and core instrumentalists who established the standard big band instrumentation and repertoire. The network reflects the intense professional interconnectivity of the Harlem Renaissance jazz scene, where musicians frequently rotated through the houses of Henderson, Ellington, and Calloway.

items.label: 1948-1997 New Orleans Jazz Circle

items.summary: This community consists of five individuals connected through oral history interviews conducted by Tulane University between 1948 and 1997. The group represents a tight-knit social circle of New Orleans musicians and associates active during the mid-to-late 20th century, likely involved in the preservation and performance of traditional jazz styles.

items.label: Classical Conductors & Impresarios
items.scene: High-art classical music and cultural patronage
items.summary: This community is dominated by European and American classical musicians, conductors, and impresarios rather than jazz performers. The connections likely stem from oral histories where interviewees discussed their exposure to high culture, prestigious orchestras, or the broader artistic elite of the early 20th century.

items.label: Modern British Jazz Collective
items.scene: Contemporary British jazz and percussion ensemble
items.summary: This community represents a tight-knit circle of contemporary British jazz musicians, heavily centered around the London scene. The group is defined by the collaborative network of percussionist Paul Clarvis and pianist Alcyona Mick, who are frequent collaborators in modern British jazz ensembles, with connections extending to younger musicians like James Maddren.

items.label: 1948-1997 New Orleans Oral History

items.summary: This community consists of three individuals identified solely through mentions in Tulane University's oral history interviews conducted between 1948 and 1997. The connections are derived exclusively from interview narratives describing personal or professional associations within the New Orleans jazz ecosystem.
